Reports from HRW, Amnesty International, and UN experts document torture in DGRE (intelligence service) facilities, military detention, and during counter-terrorism operations against both Anglophone separatists and Boko Haram suspects.

laws.title: Sanaga River Hydropower System
laws.subtitle: Edéa, Song Loulou, and New Hydropower Dams
laws.fullDescription: The Sanaga River — Cameroon's largest river — provides the backbone of the country's hydropower system. Existing dams (Edéa, Song Loulou) have generated power since the colonial era. New projects including Nachtigal HPP (420 MW) — financed by IFC and international banks — are under construction. The Lom Pangar Dam (hydropower + reservoir) has increased water storage for downstream power stations. Hydropower provides over 75% of Cameroon's electricity. Environmental impact assessments for new dams have been required by international lenders, improving standards.
laws.penalty: Interference with dam operations: criminal prosecution; downstream pollution of Sanaga River: environmental prosecution; unauthorized water extraction from regulated sections: fines
exceptions: Emergency draw-down operations for dam safety authorized without standard environmental review
Small-scale irrigation below threshold volumes from tributaries under simplified permit

quiz.q: What percentage of Cameroon's electricity comes from hydropower?
quiz.explanation: Hydropower provides over 75% of Cameroon's electricity — making it heavily dependent on rainfall and river flows. The Sanaga River system (Edéa, Song Loulou, and the new Nachtigal project) plus the Bini River projects form the core of the power system. The Lom Pangar reservoir was built specifically to regulate dry-season water flow to downstream power stations.

laws.title: Agricultural Development Bank
laws.subtitle: ACEFA and Smallholder Farmer Credit
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's agricultural sector employs over 60% of the workforce but remains largely subsistence-level. Access to credit for smallholder farmers is extremely limited — commercial banks avoid agricultural lending due to risk and informality. The ACEFA program (Support for Family Farming Competitiveness) provided subsidized inputs, training, and credit to smallholders. CAMCCUL (Cameroon Cooperative Credit Union League) provides cooperative banking services including agricultural loans. The lack of land titles for most smallholders makes them ineligible for formal bank credit even where available.
laws.penalty: Agricultural input subsidy fraud: criminal prosecution; cooperative credit fraud: civil and criminal liability; falsifying farm ownership for credit: fraud prosecution
exceptions: Cooperative member loans under CAMCCUL use social collateral — no land title required
Emergency agricultural credit during drought or flood may waive standard requirements

quiz.q: Why can most Cameroonian smallholders not access formal bank credit?
options: Banks are not interested in any agricultural lending
Smallholders lack land titles that banks require as collateral
Government prohibits agricultural lending by banks
Smallholders earn too much for poverty programs but too little for banks
quiz.explanation: Most Cameroonian smallholder farmers lack formal land titles — relying instead on customary land rights — which disqualifies them from commercial bank credit that requires titled land as collateral. This credit access gap keeps most agricultural production at subsistence level, limiting investment in inputs, equipment, and productivity improvements.

laws.title: Higher Education and University System
laws.subtitle: University of Yaoundé and Research Capacity
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon has eight state universities — including the University of Yaoundé I and II, the University of Douala, Buea (Anglophone), Dschang, Ngaoundéré, Maroua, and Bamenda (Anglophone). The bilingual dual-system (French and English universities) reflects Cameroon's language division. Brain drain severely affects Cameroonian universities — top graduates and professors emigrate to Europe and North America. Research output is limited. Fees are modest but infrastructure, library resources, and academic support are chronically underfunded. The Bamenda and Buea universities in the conflict zone have been severely disrupted.
laws.penalty: Academic fraud including degree falsification: criminal prosecution; unauthorized university operation: closure and fines; bribery of professors: corruption prosecution
exceptions: Private universities accredited by MINESUP may award state-recognized degrees under framework agreements
Distance learning institutions under MINESUP oversight have simplified physical infrastructure requirements

quiz.q: How have Cameroon's Anglophone universities been affected by the crisis?
options: They have expanded with increased government funding
The University of Buea and Bamenda have been severely disrupted by ghost town strikes and conflict
quiz.explanation: The Universities of Buea and Bamenda — in the Anglophone Southwest and Northwest regions respectively — have been severely disrupted by the Anglophone crisis. Ghost town (ville morte) strikes enforced by separatists have repeatedly shut campuses; military operations and population displacement have affected academic calendars, faculty, and students for years.

laws.title: Human Rights Commission CNDHL
laws.subtitle: National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms
laws.fullDescription: The National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms (CNDHL) is Cameroon's national human rights institution, established in 2004. The CNDHL has the mandate to investigate complaints, conduct prison visits, and report on human rights situations. In practice, the CNDHL has been criticized for limited independence — its members are government-appointed and it rarely challenges security force abuses. International organizations have given it a 'B' status rating (partially compliant) with the Paris Principles for national human rights institutions. The Anglophone crisis has tested the CNDHL's independence and capacity.
laws.penalty: Interference with CNDHL mandate: administrative sanction; obstruction of prison visits: contempt; torture complaints documented by CNDHL: subject to prosecution referral
exceptions: Military installation visits require security clearance even for CNDHL delegates
CNDHL confidential informant protection provisions shield complaint sources

quiz.q: What is the CNDHL's Paris Principles compliance rating?
options: B status — partially compliant due to limited independence
Not rated by the Paris Principles system
quiz.explanation: Cameroon's CNDHL (National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms) holds a 'B' status rating under the Paris Principles — indicating partial compliance with international standards for national human rights institutions. The main concerns are limited independence from government control and insufficient capacity to independently investigate security force abuses.

laws.title: Financial Crime and Embezzlement
laws.subtitle: TCS and Public Finance Prosecutions
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's Special Criminal Court (TCS — Tribunal Criminel Spécial) was established in 2011 to handle corruption and public fund embezzlement cases above CFA 50 million. The TCS has prosecuted numerous high-profile cases — including former ministers, governors, and directors of state enterprises. Under Operation Épervier, over 50 senior officials have been convicted. Critics note that prosecutions track political developments — those who fall out of favor with Biya are prosecuted while allies are protected. The TCS has expanded its capacity over the years.
laws.penalty: Public fund embezzlement over CFA 50M: 15–25 years (TCS jurisdiction); bribery: 5–20 years; abuse of public office for private gain: 10–20 years
exceptions: Presidential immunity for official acts — though former presidents have no immunity once out of office
International diplomatic immunity for foreign officials — waivable by home country

quiz.q: What is the threshold for TCS jurisdiction in Cameroon?
options: Any amount of public fund embezzlement
All government official corruption regardless of amount
quiz.explanation: The Special Criminal Court (TCS) in Cameroon has jurisdiction over corruption and embezzlement cases involving public funds above CFA 50 million (approximately USD 80,000). Cases below this threshold go to regular courts. The threshold was set to focus TCS resources on significant financial crimes while allowing lower-level cases to be handled through ordinary judicial channels.

laws.title: CBD Biodiversity Strategy
laws.subtitle: National Biodiversity Strategy and REDD+
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) aligns with the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). Cameroon is a biodiversity hotspot — with exceptional endemic species in the Cameroon Highlands, Congo Basin rainforest, and coastal zones. REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation) programs have attracted carbon finance for forest conservation. The Tri-National Sangha transboundary park (shared with Congo and CAR) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Conservation faces pressure from agricultural expansion, illegal logging, and mining.
laws.penalty: Violating protected species permits: criminal prosecution; unauthorized REDD+ carbon trading: fraud prosecution; destruction of UNESCO heritage site: maximum environmental penalties
exceptions: REDD+ benefit sharing agreements with local communities create legal rights to compensation
Traditional community use of biodiversity under Nagoya Protocol prior informed consent

quiz.q: What is the Tri-National Sangha and why is it significant?
options: A border dispute zone between three countries
A transboundary UNESCO World Heritage park shared by Cameroon, Congo, and CAR
A mining concession zone shared by three countries
quiz.explanation: The Tri-National Sangha (TNS) is a transboundary protected area and UNESCO World Heritage Site shared between Cameroon, the Republic of Congo, and the Central African Republic. It covers over 750,000 hectares of intact Congo Basin rainforest, harboring forest elephants, western lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, and extraordinary biodiversity.

laws.title: Religious Diversity and Freedom
laws.subtitle: Christians, Muslims, and Traditional Religions
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon has remarkable religious diversity — approximately 40% Christian (Catholic, Protestant, Evangelical), 20% Muslim (concentrated in the north), and 40% traditional African religions (many people practice combinations). The constitution guarantees religious freedom. Religious harmony is generally good — interfaith marriages are common in southern Cameroon. The northern Muslim communities have distinct legal traditions in some areas of personal law. Religious extremism risk exists in the Far North (Boko Haram influence). Religious organizations operate schools and hospitals that supplement the public sector.
laws.penalty: Religious persecution: criminal prosecution under freedom of religion provisions; inciting religious violence: 10–20 years; unauthorized religious organization operation: administrative sanctions
exceptions: Established churches and mosques operate under simplified registration compared to new religious movements
Religious personal law for marriage and inheritance recognized in northern communities under customary provisions

quiz.q: What is the approximate religious composition of Cameroon?
quiz.explanation: Cameroon has remarkable religious diversity: approximately 40% Christian (spread across Catholic, Protestant, and Evangelical denominations), 20% Muslim (concentrated in the North and Far North regions), and 40% traditional African religions — though many Cameroonians practice syncretic combinations of Christian or Muslim faith with traditional practices.

laws.title: Mining Code and Mineral Resources
laws.subtitle: Artisanal Mining and Industrial Concessions
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's Mining Code (2016) governs artisanal, small-scale, and industrial mining. Cameroon has significant mineral resources: bauxite (Minim-Martap — one of the world's largest reserves), iron ore (Mbalam), cobalt, nickel, and diamonds. Industrial development has been slow due to infrastructure deficits (particularly railway connections to mineral deposits). Artisanal mining employs hundreds of thousands — particularly in gold, diamond, and coltan extraction — with significant informal activity. Chinese companies have secured several mining concessions.
laws.penalty: Artisanal mining without permit: fines and equipment confiscation; operating beyond concession boundaries: criminal prosecution; environmental damage from mining: heavy fines and remediation orders
exceptions: Artisanal miners in designated artisanal zones may operate under simplified permit
Community mining cooperatives in defined areas have reduced royalty rates under social mining provisions

quiz.q: What is the significance of Minim-Martap in Cameroon's mining sector?
options: One of the world's largest bauxite reserves (aluminum ore)
quiz.explanation: Minim-Martap in northern Cameroon contains one of the world's largest untapped bauxite reserves (aluminum ore). Despite the enormous potential, development has been constrained by infrastructure challenges — particularly the lack of a rail connection to transport the heavy ore to the coast for export. Several foreign companies have held concessions, but large-scale extraction has not yet begun.

laws.title: Refugee Hosting Obligations
laws.subtitle: UNHCR and Central African Refugees
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon hosts over 450,000 refugees — predominantly from the Central African Republic (CAR) and Nigeria. CAR refugees flee recurring armed conflict in their country; Nigerian refugees are primarily from Boko Haram-affected Borno State. The East region hosts the largest CAR refugee population; the Adamawa region hosts Nigerians. Cameroon itself is a conflict producer — generating Anglophone IDPs and refugees in Nigeria. UNHCR, WFP, and NGOs provide humanitarian assistance. The government generally respects the non-refoulement principle, though conditions for refugees are challenging.
laws.penalty: Forced refoulement of refugees to persecution: violation of 1951 Refugee Convention; unauthorized refugee camps outside designated areas: administrative action
exceptions: Prima facie refugee status granted to CAR and Nigerian refugees under group determination procedure
Refugees with skills needed by Cameroon may receive work authorization under special provision

quiz.q: From which two countries do most of Cameroon's 450,000+ refugees originate?
quiz.explanation: Cameroon hosts over 450,000 refugees, predominantly from the Central African Republic (fleeing recurring armed conflict) and Nigeria (fleeing Boko Haram in Borno State). The East region of Cameroon hosts the largest CAR refugee population, while the Adamawa region receives Nigerian refugees — creating a complex humanitarian situation where Cameroon is simultaneously a refugee host and a conflict-affected country.

laws.title: Road Traffic Laws
laws.subtitle: MINTRANSPORT and Road Safety
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon has one of Africa's highest rates of road traffic accidents — inadequate road infrastructure, overloaded vehicles, driver fatigue (long-distance buses), and poor vehicle maintenance are primary causes. The Yaoundé-Bafoussam road is notoriously dangerous. MINTRANSPORT regulates vehicle standards, driver licensing, and road transport companies. Intercity buses (agencies) are the primary mode of long-distance travel for most Cameroonians. Speed limits, seatbelt requirements, and vehicle roadworthiness standards are legally required but poorly enforced.
laws.penalty: Causing death by dangerous driving: 5–15 years; drunk driving: 1–5 years; operating unroadworthy commercial vehicle: fines and vehicle impoundment; driving without license: fines
exceptions: Agricultural vehicles (tractors) operating within farm boundaries exempt from road licensing
Emergency vehicles responding to incidents authorized to exceed speed limits

quiz.q: What is a major cause of Cameroon's high road traffic accident rate?
options: Very high car ownership creating congestion
Inadequate road infrastructure, overloaded vehicles, driver fatigue, and poor maintenance
quiz.explanation: Cameroon's high road accident rate results from multiple factors: inadequate road infrastructure (many roads are unpaved or poorly maintained), overloaded intercity buses, driver fatigue on long routes, poor vehicle maintenance, and limited traffic law enforcement. The Yaoundé-Bafoussam route through mountains is particularly dangerous, with frequent fatal accidents.

laws.title: Decentralization and Regional Councils
laws.subtitle: 2019 Regional Elections and Special Status Implementation
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon held its first-ever regional elections in December 2019 — fulfilling a long-delayed constitutional requirement for elected regional assemblies. The regions include the two Anglophone regions (with their special status) plus eight Francophone regions. Regional councils have limited powers — mainly planning, culture, and local development. RDPC dominates most regional councils. The Southwest and Northwest regional councils represent a milestone for Anglophone governance — though separatists boycotted the elections. FEICOM (Inter-communal Fund for Equipment) channels funds to local councils.
laws.penalty: Electoral fraud in regional elections: 5–15 years; unauthorized assumption of regional council powers: administrative sanction; corruption in FEICOM fund disbursement: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Traditional rulers (chefs traditionnels) have advisory roles within regional councils under custom
FEICOM emergency disbursements for disaster relief bypass standard council approval

quiz.q: When did Cameroon hold its first-ever regional council elections?
options: December 2019 — fulfilling a long-delayed constitutional requirement
quiz.explanation: Cameroon held its first regional elections in December 2019 — more than two decades after the constitutional requirement for elected regional assemblies was established. The elections were seen as a concession following the Anglophone crisis, providing the new special status regions with elected representative bodies, though their actual powers remain limited.

laws.title: Medicinal Plants and Traditional Medicine
laws.subtitle: IMPM and Traditional Health Regulation
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's forests contain thousands of medicinal plant species used in traditional medicine practiced by herbalists, traditional healers, and nganga (spiritualists). IMPM (Institute of Medical Research and Medicinal Plants) researches and standardizes traditional medicines. The Traditional Medicine Practitioners' Association works toward professionalization. Traditional medicine provides primary healthcare for up to 80% of the population in rural areas. Biopiracy concerns have emerged — pharmaceutical companies accessing traditional knowledge without fair compensation under Nagoya Protocol obligations.
laws.penalty: Biopiracy — commercial exploitation of traditional knowledge without prior informed consent: criminal prosecution and benefit-sharing orders; practicing traditional medicine without registration: administrative fines
exceptions: Traditional healers practicing within their community under traditional authority recognized without formal registration
Research use of traditional knowledge under prior informed consent and benefit-sharing agreement

quiz.q: What percentage of Cameroonians in rural areas rely on traditional medicine as primary healthcare?
quiz.explanation: Traditional medicine provides primary healthcare for up to 80% of the population in rural Cameroon — making traditional healers, herbalists, and nganga the de facto primary care system for most rural communities. This reality drives government efforts to regulate, research, and integrate traditional medicine into the health system through IMPM.

laws.title: Industrialization Strategy — SND30
laws.subtitle: Structural Transformation and Value Addition
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's SND30 (National Development Strategy 2020-2030) targets structural transformation — shifting from primary commodity exports toward value-added manufacturing. Key sectors: agro-industry (processed cocoa, coffee, timber products), aluminum smelting (ALUCAM — using low-cost hydropower), cement, and textiles. ALUCAM (aluminum smelter at Edéa) converts imported alumina into aluminum using cheap Sanaga River hydroelectricity — representing a successful value-addition model. Industrial zones (Bassa, Bonabéri in Douala) house manufacturing operations.
laws.penalty: Operating industrial facility without environmental permit: fines and shutdown; violation of product quality standards: market prohibition; industrial espionage: criminal prosecution
exceptions: SMEs in industrial zones benefit from simplified permit procedures under SND30 SME promotion
Export-oriented manufacturers in EPZs exempt from some domestic trade regulations

quiz.q: What product does ALUCAM produce at Edéa using Sanaga River hydroelectricity?
options: Aluminum — converting imported alumina using cheap hydroelectric power
quiz.explanation: ALUCAM (Aluminium du Cameroun) at Edéa smelts aluminum — converting imported alumina (aluminum oxide) into aluminum metal using the cheap hydroelectric power from the Sanaga River's Edéa dam. This represents one of Cameroon's successful value-addition industries — taking advantage of abundant clean energy to create a higher-value export product.

laws.title: Nutrition and Food Security
laws.subtitle: MINADER/WFP Programs and Malnutrition
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon faces significant nutrition challenges — chronic malnutrition affects nearly 30% of children under 5, with stunting particularly high in the Far North region (where Boko Haram conflict, drought, and poverty converge) and the Anglophone conflict regions. The WFP (World Food Programme) and UNICEF support government nutrition programs including therapeutic feeding centers, school feeding programs, and micronutrient supplementation. MINADER coordinates agricultural programs aimed at food security. Urban food security in Douala and Yaoundé is also challenged by high food prices.
laws.penalty: Food aid diversion: criminal prosecution; operating nutrition programs without MINSANTE authorization: fines; adulteration of infant formula: 10 years
exceptions: Emergency feeding programs during declared humanitarian crises may operate under simplified WHO/UNICEF emergency authorization
Community kitchen gardens on unregistered urban plots allowed under food security exception

quiz.q: Which Cameroonian region has the highest child malnutrition rates?
options: The Far North region (Boko Haram conflict, drought, poverty)
quiz.explanation: The Far North region of Cameroon has the highest child malnutrition rates — combining multiple crises: active Boko Haram conflict, recurring drought and climate change impacts, extreme poverty, and disrupted food systems. Stunting rates in the Far North significantly exceed the national average of ~30% for children under 5.

laws.title: Criminal Procedure Code 2005
laws.subtitle: CPC Reforms and Due Process Rights
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's 2005 Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) modernized the colonial-era criminal procedure framework. Key reforms included habeas corpus provisions, legal aid access, time limits on pretrial detention, and rights to interpretation. In practice, many CPC rights are poorly implemented: legal aid is minimal, interpretation is inadequate, and pretrial detention far exceeds legal limits for many defendants. The Anglophone conflict has created a category of defendants tried in military courts outside CPC protections. Bar associations in both Anglophone and Francophone regions provide legal representation.
laws.penalty: Illegal detention beyond CPC limits: officer liability; evidence obtained through torture excluded: judges have power to exclude; coerced confessions: criminal prosecution of officers
exceptions: National security detention under administrative order bypasses CPC time limits for up to 15 days (renewable)
Military tribunal procedures differ from civilian CPC

quiz.q: What key reform did Cameroon's 2005 Criminal Procedure Code introduce?
options: It eliminated all detention time limits
Introduction of habeas corpus, legal aid access, interpretation rights, and pretrial detention time limits
It merged Anglophone common law with Francophone civil procedure
quiz.explanation: Cameroon's 2005 Criminal Procedure Code introduced important due process reforms including habeas corpus provisions, legal aid access, rights to interpretation (critical in a multilingual country), and legal time limits on pretrial detention. Despite these reforms, implementation is weak — many defendants still experience conditions far below the CPC's intended standards.

laws.title: Coastal Zone Management
laws.subtitle: Mangroves, Coastal Erosion, and Sea Level Rise
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's 402 km Atlantic coastline includes vital mangrove ecosystems (particularly the Wouri estuary around Douala), coastal wetlands, and sandy beaches. Mangroves provide nursery habitat for fisheries, storm protection, and carbon sequestration. Urban expansion of Douala into mangrove areas is a major threat. Coastal erosion affects several communities. Sea level rise projections indicate significant threat to low-lying coastal areas including parts of Douala — a city of 3+ million. MINEPDED coordinates coastal zone management.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized mangrove clearing: criminal prosecution; industrial development in coastal protected zones without EIA: fines and suspension; illegal sand extraction: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Fishing communities with traditional landing sites in coastal protected zones have use rights
Emergency coastal infrastructure repair after storms may proceed without standard EIA under expedited review

quiz.q: Why are Wouri estuary mangroves significant for Cameroon?
options: They are purely aesthetic — no economic value
They provide nursery habitat for fisheries, storm protection, and carbon sequestration near Douala
They are the only mangroves in West Africa
They contain rare medicinal plants found nowhere else
quiz.explanation: The Wouri estuary mangroves around Douala serve multiple critical functions: providing nursery habitat for the Gulf of Guinea fisheries that support thousands of fishing families, protecting Douala's coastline from storm surges, and sequestering significant amounts of carbon as a 'blue carbon' ecosystem. Urban expansion into these mangroves threatens all these services simultaneously.

laws.title: Bamileke Cultural and Economic Power
laws.subtitle: Grassfields Chieftaincies and Business Networks
laws.fullDescription: The Bamileke people — from the West Region's Grassfields — are one of Cameroon's most economically dynamic ethnic groups. Despite historical marginalization by colonial powers, Bamileke have become dominant in Cameroon's informal and formal business sector. Bamileke traditional chieftaincy (fon) systems remain politically important. Bamileke diaspora networks within Cameroon and internationally support entrepreneurship. The SDF (Social Democratic Front) opposition party has historically drawn strong Bamileke and Anglophone support. Bamileke culture includes famous palace arts — masks, royal regalia — protected as cultural heritage.
laws.penalty: Cultural heritage theft — Bamileke royal artifacts: criminal prosecution and repatriation orders; unauthorized commercialization of traditional titles: customary law violation
exceptions: Traditional fon courts may adjudicate intra-community disputes under customary law with limited formal recognition
Bamileke palace festivals and ceremonies exempt from standard public gathering permit requirements

quiz.q: What is a 'fon' in Bamileke tradition?
options: A traditional chief or king of a chieftaincy — with significant political and cultural authority
quiz.explanation: A 'fon' is a traditional chief or king in Bamileke (and other Grassfields) chieftaincy systems — exercising significant cultural, political, and sometimes judicial authority over their community. Fon systems remain relevant in modern Cameroon, with fons consulted on development projects, conflict resolution, and community governance in the West Region.

laws.title: Natural Gas Development
laws.subtitle: GASCAM and Offshore Gas Reserves
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon has significant natural gas reserves — associated gas from oil production and deepwater gas fields offshore. GASCAM (Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures Gas Branch) manages gas development. Domestic gas use for power generation has grown — the Kribi gas-fired power plant uses offshore gas. Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) export potential exists but requires major infrastructure investment. Gas flaring from oil operations — an environmental waste — has been reduced through regulatory requirements. Cameroon's gas sector could grow significantly if infrastructure investment materializes.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized gas extraction: criminal prosecution; gas flaring beyond permitted levels: fines and equipment shutdown; pipeline safety violations: criminal prosecution of operators
exceptions: Safety flaring during emergency pressure release authorized without permit
Research drilling for gas under exploration license before production regulations apply

quiz.q: What significant gas infrastructure operates at Kribi in Cameroon?
options: A gas-fired power plant using offshore natural gas
A major gas pipeline to Nigeria
A gas processing plant for European export
quiz.explanation: The Kribi gas-fired power plant uses offshore natural gas from Cameroon's Gulf of Guinea fields to generate electricity — representing an important step in domestic gas utilization. The plant adds to Cameroon's electricity generation capacity and reduces dependence on hydropower during dry seasons when river levels affect hydroelectric output.

laws.title: Civil Service and Public Administration
laws.subtitle: MINATD and Fonctionnaires Governance
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's civil service (fonction publique) employs over 300,000 fonctionnaires. The General Statute of Civil Servants governs employment, promotion, discipline, and retirement. MINATD (Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralization) coordinates administrative governance. The civil service is administered through French and English-speaking parallel tracks in many ministries. Political appointments are heavily influenced by ethnic, regional, and political balancing. Ghost workers (fictitious employees drawing salaries) are a documented problem. The SIGIPES payroll system was introduced to improve control.
laws.penalty: Ghost worker fraud: criminal prosecution and salary recovery; civil service bribery: 5–15 years; unauthorized strike by essential services employees: disciplinary action
exceptions: Contract employees (contractuels) governed by Labor Code not Civil Service Statute
Specialized employees (medical, technical) may have separate employment frameworks

quiz.q: What is the SIGIPES system in Cameroon's civil service?
options: A payroll management system introduced to control ghost worker fraud
quiz.explanation: SIGIPES (Système Intégré de Gestion des Personnels de l'État et de la Solde) is Cameroon's integrated civil service payroll management system — introduced to control the significant ghost worker problem where fictitious employees drew government salaries. The system centralizes personnel records and payroll to identify and remove fraudulent entries.

laws.title: Malaria Control Programs
laws.subtitle: PNLP and Bed Net Distribution
laws.fullDescription: Malaria is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Cameroon — particularly for children under 5 and pregnant women. The PNLP (Programme National de Lutte contre le Paludisme) coordinates national malaria control. Mass distribution of insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, and artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) have reduced mortality. However, malaria incidence remains very high — Cameroon has among the highest malaria burdens in Africa. Global Fund and PMI (US President's Malaria Initiative) provide significant financial support.
laws.penalty: Selling counterfeit antimalarial drugs: 10–20 years; bed net diversion from public programs: criminal prosecution; unregistered malaria treatment products: market prohibition
exceptions: Traditional antimalarial plant remedies — particularly Artemisia annua tea — used in community settings without pharmaceutical licensing
Emergency malaria treatment during outbreak may use unregistered drugs under Ministry authorization

quiz.q: What financing sources support Cameroon's malaria control program?
options: The Global Fund and PMI (US President's Malaria Initiative) alongside government
quiz.explanation: Cameroon's malaria control program receives significant support from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria and the US President's Malaria Initiative (PMI) — alongside Cameroonian government funding. These international partners fund bed net distributions, antimalarial drugs (ACTs), and health system capacity building that Cameroon could not afford alone.

laws.title: International Criminal Court and Cameroon
laws.subtitle: Rome Statute and ICC Jurisdiction
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon ratified the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court in 2010 — giving the ICC jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes committed in Cameroon. The Anglophone conflict has raised questions about ICC jurisdiction — with human rights organizations documenting potential war crimes by both government forces and armed separatists. No formal ICC investigation into Cameroon has been opened. The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber's preliminary examination process has been discussed. Cameroon's ratification theoretically allows Cameroonian victims to petition the ICC if domestic remedies fail.
laws.penalty: War crimes under Rome Statute: ICC prosecution and sentences up to life imprisonment; crimes against humanity: ICC jurisdiction; genocide: maximum penalties under Rome Statute
exceptions: Head of state immunity — though the ICC has charged sitting heads of state before
Complementarity principle: ICC only acts if Cameroon fails to genuinely prosecute war crimes nationally

quiz.q: What is the complementarity principle for ICC jurisdiction in Cameroon?
options: ICC automatically takes cases without national courts involved
ICC only acts if Cameroon fails to genuinely prosecute war crimes and atrocities nationally
ICC has no jurisdiction in African countries
quiz.explanation: The complementarity principle means the ICC only exercises jurisdiction over cases in Cameroon if Cameroon fails or is unwilling to genuinely prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, or genocide at the national level. This principle preserves national sovereignty while ensuring accountability — theoretically incentivizing states to prosecute rather than shield perpetrators.

laws.title: Social Protection Programs
laws.subtitle: MINAS and Vulnerable Population Support
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's social protection system — managed by MINAS (Ministry of Social Affairs) — provides limited support for vulnerable populations: orphans, elderly without family support, persons with disabilities, and extreme poor. The Bourse de Sécurité Familiale (BSF) conditional cash transfer program, supported by the World Bank, provides small cash transfers to extremely poor households. Coverage is extremely limited relative to need. Pension systems (CNPS) cover only formal sector workers — leaving most Cameroonians without retirement protection. Social protection expansion is a priority under SND30.
laws.penalty: Social protection fraud: criminal prosecution and repayment; exploitation of vulnerable persons registered with MINAS: criminal prosecution; CNPS contribution evasion by employers: fines and back payment
exceptions: Informal sector self-employed workers may voluntarily join CNPS under special membership provisions
Social protection programs during declared national emergencies may expand eligibility criteria

quiz.q: What is the BSF program in Cameroon?
options: Bourse de Sécurité Familiale — a conditional cash transfer program for the extreme poor
A scholarship for secondary school students
quiz.explanation: The Bourse de Sécurité Familiale (BSF) is a World Bank-supported conditional cash transfer program providing small cash payments to extremely poor Cameroonian households — typically conditioned on school attendance and health checkups for children. Coverage is limited relative to need, but the program represents a building block for expanding social protection.

laws.title: Palm Oil and Deforestation
laws.subtitle: EU Deforestation Regulation and Cameroon Compliance
laws.fullDescription: Palm oil production is expanding in Cameroon — with large concessions by industrial producers and smallholder outgrowers. Palm oil expansion threatens Congo Basin forest — particularly in the southwest (Mungo area). The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), effective 2024, requires all palm oil (and other commodities) entering the EU to be certified deforestation-free. Cameroon companies exporting to Europe must demonstrate their supply chains are not linked to deforestation. This creates compliance challenges for smallholder-sourced palm oil. RSPO (Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil) certified production is growing but remains minority.
laws.penalty: Clearing protected forest for palm oil: criminal prosecution and land restoration order; EUDR non-compliance affecting EU market access: trade suspension; fraudulent deforestation-free certificates: criminal fraud prosecution
exceptions: Smallholder outgrowers under certified company supply chains benefit from group certification
Historical plantations pre-dating forest protection legislation may operate under transition provisions

quiz.q: What does the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) require of Cameroon palm oil exporters?
options: Pay a deforestation tax on all exports
Certification that supply chains are not linked to deforestation — or lose EU market access
Only large companies affected — smallholders are exempt
quiz.explanation: The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) requires all palm oil (and other commodities like cocoa, timber, and rubber) entering the EU market to be certified as deforestation-free. Cameroonian exporters must demonstrate through due diligence that their supply chains are not linked to forest clearing — or risk losing access to EU markets, their most valuable export destination.

laws.title: Hostage-Taking and Kidnap for Ransom
laws.subtitle: Kidnapping Crisis and Security Forces Response
laws.fullDescription: Kidnapping for ransom has become a significant security problem in Cameroon — with incidents in multiple regions. In the Northwest and Southwest (Anglophone regions), armed separatist groups abduct teachers, businesspeople, and others for ransom. In the Far North, Boko Haram has used abductions. In the East and South, criminality-driven kidnappings occur. The government has struggled to address the epidemic. School abductions in the Anglophone region — including the October 2018 Bamenda kidnapping of schoolchildren — have received international attention.
laws.penalty: Kidnapping for ransom: 20 years to life; kidnapping of children: life imprisonment; organizing kidnapping network: death penalty; paying ransom (theoretically illegal but rarely prosecuted): civil forfeiture risk
exceptions: Ransom payments under duress by victims or families treated as extorted — not criminal for payers in practice
Undercover law enforcement operations against kidnapping networks authorized under judicial warrant

quiz.q: What high-profile kidnapping incident in October 2018 drew international attention to Cameroon?
options: Kidnapping of schoolchildren in Bamenda by armed separatists
Abduction of Catholic priests in the Far North
quiz.explanation: In October 2018, armed separatists abducted 79 students and 3 teachers from Presbyterian Secondary School in Bamenda, Northwest Region — drawing widespread international condemnation. The children were released after a few days, but the incident highlighted how the Anglophone conflict was threatening education and targeting children.

laws.title: Banking Sector Regulations
laws.subtitle: COBAC and BEAC Supervision
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's banking sector is supervised by COBAC (Commission Bancaire de l'Afrique Centrale) — the regional banking supervisor for all CEMAC countries. Major banks include Société Générale Cameroun, Afriland First Bank, SCB Cameroun, Ecobank, and others. Banking penetration is approximately 20% — most Cameroonians are unbanked. Mobile money (MTN MoMo, Orange Money) has expanded financial access beyond banks. Microfinance institutions (MFIs) serve small businesses and low-income households — regulated by MINFI. The banking sector remained stable through recent economic pressures.
laws.penalty: Banking fraud: 5–20 years; operating unlicensed deposit-taking institution: criminal prosecution and asset seizure; market manipulation: COBAC sanctions and criminal prosecution
exceptions: Credit unions (credit unions coopératives) under CAMCCUL have simplified COBAC registration
Savings groups (tontines — informal rotating credit) not regulated as formal financial institutions

quiz.q: What is COBAC and what is its role in Cameroon's banking sector?
options: Commission Bancaire de l'Afrique Centrale — the regional banking supervisor for all CEMAC countries
A French banking regulatory body with jurisdiction in former colonies
quiz.explanation: COBAC (Commission Bancaire de l'Afrique Centrale) is the regional banking supervisor for all six CEMAC countries including Cameroon. Rather than each country having its own banking supervisor, the shared COBAC model reflects CEMAC's monetary integration. COBAC licenses banks, conducts on-site inspections, and can withdraw banking licenses for regulatory violations.

laws.title: Ebola Preparedness and Epidemic Response
laws.subtitle: COUSP and Emergency Health Protocols
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon borders both Nigeria (which has experienced Ebola cases) and the Central African Republic (which borders DRC — the Ebola epicenter). Cameroon has invested in epidemic preparedness since 2014. The COUSP (Emergency Operations Center for Public Health) coordinates outbreak response. During COVID-19, Cameroon declared a state of health emergency — implementing curfews, closing schools, and mandating masks. COVID-19 vaccination lagged due to vaccine availability and hesitancy. Cameroon has participated in WHO IHR Joint External Evaluation to assess preparedness.
laws.penalty: Violating quarantine orders during declared epidemic: criminal prosecution; concealing epidemic symptoms at border: fines; obstructing epidemic response: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Essential service workers (medical, security, food supply) exempt from epidemic-related movement restrictions
Humanitarian emergency shipments exempt from import restrictions during health crisis

quiz.q: Why is Cameroon at particular risk for Ebola spillover?
options: Cameroon has already had Ebola outbreaks
It borders Nigeria (Ebola cases) and CAR (bordering DRC — the Ebola epicenter)
Cameroon has bats carrying Ebola throughout the country
quiz.explanation: Cameroon faces elevated Ebola spillover risk due to its geographic position — bordering Nigeria (which has experienced sporadic Ebola cases) and the Central African Republic (which borders the DRC, the country with the world's most Ebola outbreaks). This border geography drives Cameroon's investment in cross-border health surveillance and epidemic preparedness.

laws.title: Judiciary Independence
laws.subtitle: Supreme Court and Administrative Courts
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's judiciary — comprising the Supreme Court, Courts of Appeal, High Courts, and administrative tribunals — faces chronic challenges to independence. Judicial appointments are made by the President through the Superior Council of Magistracy (CSM). The CSM was recently reformed to include more judicial representation, but presidential influence remains dominant. Pay is low, caseloads are crushing, and judicial infrastructure is poor. Corruption in the judiciary is documented — parties with means can influence outcomes. Judicial decisions in politically sensitive cases routinely favor the government.
laws.penalty: Judicial corruption: 10–20 years; contempt of court: fines and detention; perverting course of justice: 5–15 years; intimidating witnesses: 3–10 years
exceptions: Constitutional Council members have immunity for judicial acts during their mandate
Military tribunal judges governed by military regulations rather than civilian judicial statute

quiz.q: What body controls judicial appointments in Cameroon?
options: The Superior Council of Magistracy (CSM) — where presidential influence is dominant
Parliament votes on all judicial appointments
quiz.explanation: Judicial appointments in Cameroon are made through the Superior Council of Magistracy (CSM), where the President of the Republic plays a dominant role. Despite reforms adding more judicial representation, presidential influence over judicial appointments — combined with low pay and political pressure — fundamentally compromises judicial independence.

laws.title: Trade Facilitation and Customs
laws.subtitle: DGD and CAMCIS Customs Modernization
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's customs (Direction Générale des Douanes — DGD) is modernizing through CAMCIS (Cameroon Customs Information System), automating declarations and reducing manual intervention opportunities for corruption. Cameroon participates in the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA). Customs corruption at the Port of Douala was legendary — though improvement has occurred with electronic systems. Free zones and EPZs have simplified customs procedures for qualifying exporters. Transit procedures for goods destined to landlocked neighbors are a priority.
laws.penalty: Customs fraud: fines of 3× the value of goods; smuggling: criminal prosecution and goods confiscation; customs official corruption: 10–15 years
exceptions: ATA carnet system for temporary import of professional equipment without customs payment
Diplomatic goods under Vienna Convention exempt from customs inspection and duties

quiz.q: What is CAMCIS in Cameroon's customs modernization?
options: Cameroon Customs Information System — automating declarations to reduce corruption
quiz.explanation: CAMCIS (Cameroon Customs Information System) is the electronic customs management platform modernizing Cameroon's customs administration. By automating cargo declarations and risk assessment, CAMCIS reduces opportunities for the manual, face-to-face corruption that has historically made Douala port one of Africa's most expensive to clear goods through.

laws.title: Tobacco Control and Health Policy
laws.subtitle: WHO FCTC and Tobacco Regulations
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon has ratified the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC). Tobacco use prevalence is moderate by global standards but growing — particularly among young urban men. Cigarette advertising is restricted. Health warning requirements on packaging are required. Tobacco taxes are used as both revenue and health policy tools. Illicit cigarette trade (smuggled products avoiding taxes) is a challenge. Smoke-free public places policies are enacted but enforcement is weak. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) — increasingly including tobacco-related cancers — are growing as a health burden.
laws.penalty: Selling tobacco to minors: fines; tobacco advertising in prohibited areas: fines; operating unregistered tobacco wholesale: business closure
exceptions: Traditional smoking of local tobacco varieties in traditional ceremonies is culturally tolerated
Shisha (hookah) cafes operate under simplified hospitality licensing without specific tobacco facility permits

quiz.q: What WHO treaty has Cameroon ratified for tobacco control?
options: WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)
quiz.explanation: Cameroon has ratified the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) — the international treaty establishing minimum standards for tobacco control policies including packaging warnings, advertising restrictions, tax measures, and smoke-free environments. Ratification commits Cameroon to these standards, though implementation quality varies.

laws.title: Plea Bargaining and TCS Procedures
laws.subtitle: Special Criminal Court Procedures
laws.fullDescription: The Special Criminal Court (TCS) in Cameroon uses procedures adapted for complex financial crime cases. The TCS introduced plea bargaining (aveu de culpabilité) provisions — allowing defendants to plead guilty in exchange for reduced sentences and asset confiscation agreements. Several high-profile Épervier defendants have used this mechanism. The TCS has expedited procedures compared to regular courts. Appeal of TCS judgments goes to the Supreme Court. International legal cooperation through GIABA (West African anti-money laundering body) and bilateral agreements supports TCS asset recovery efforts.
laws.penalty: TCS jurisdiction: embezzlement over CFA 50M — 15-25 years without plea agreement; with plea agreement: reduced to 5-15 years with cooperation; asset confiscation mandatory on conviction
exceptions: Voluntary surrender of embezzled funds before prosecution may be considered in sentencing — not a formal exception but prosecutorial practice
TCS may grant provisional release pending trial for low flight-risk defendants under electronic monitoring

quiz.q: What benefit does plea bargaining offer TCS defendants in Cameroon?
options: Reduced sentences (5-15 years vs 15-25 years) in exchange for guilty plea, cooperation, and asset confiscation
quiz.explanation: Plea bargaining at Cameroon's TCS allows defendants to plead guilty in exchange for reduced sentences — typically 5-15 years versus the standard 15-25 years — combined with agreements to return embezzled assets. Several Operation Épervier defendants have used this mechanism, which both resolves cases faster and increases asset recovery compared to contested trials.

laws.title: Groundwater and Water Resource Management
laws.subtitle: MINEE and Water Code Implementation
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's 1998 Water Law (Code de l'Eau) establishes the framework for water resource management — including groundwater, surface water, and transboundary watercourses. The MINEE (Ministry of Energy and Water) manages water policy. Groundwater provides drinking water for millions without piped water access. Artisanal hand pump maintenance is a persistent challenge — many rural water points are non-functional. Transboundary water sharing (Congo, Cross, Sanaga river basins) involves cooperation with Nigeria, CAR, DRC, and Equatorial Guinea. Water pollution from agricultural chemicals and urban runoff threatens sources.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized extraction of groundwater at commercial scale: fines; polluting drinking water sources: criminal prosecution; illegal waste disposal in water bodies: criminal prosecution and remediation orders
exceptions: Individual household wells for domestic consumption below 5 m³/day exempt from water extraction licensing
Emergency water supply during natural disaster may draw from any available source under civil protection authority

quiz.q: What year did Cameroon enact its Water Law (Code de l'Eau)?
quiz.explanation: Cameroon's Water Law (Code de l'Eau) was enacted in 1998 — establishing the legal framework for water resource management, including principles of water as a shared resource, framework for concessions and permits, environmental protection of water sources, and institutional responsibilities for the MINEE ministry and regional water authorities.

laws.title: Torture Accountability Progress
laws.subtitle: UN CAT Reviews and Domestic Prosecutions
laws.fullDescription: Despite documented torture practices, Cameroon has faced limited domestic accountability. The 2016 Penal Code criminalizes torture under Article 350. However, prosecutions of security forces for torture remain extremely rare — creating effective impunity. The UN Human Rights Committee has called for independent investigation mechanisms. Several foreign governments have conditioned security assistance on human rights improvements. Under the Anglophone conflict, credible documentation of torture has come from HRW, Amnesty, and leaked military court files. President Hassan has expressed commitment to accountability but systemic change is limited.
laws.penalty: Torture by public official under Article 350: 5–10 years; superior ordering torture: command responsibility — same penalty; covering up torture: 2–5 years
exceptions: Acts of 'legitimate coercion' in law enforcement — ambiguously defined and susceptible to abuse as justification for torture
Military classification of interrogation methods limits civilian oversight

quiz.q: Despite criminalizing torture in the 2016 Penal Code, what problem persists in Cameroon?
options: The law has too low penalties
Prosecutions of security forces for torture remain extremely rare — creating effective impunity
Torture is too difficult to prove legally
The penal code was never officially published
quiz.explanation: While Cameroon's 2016 Penal Code criminalizes torture under Article 350, prosecutions of security forces for torture in practice remain extremely rare — creating effective impunity. Documentation by HRW, Amnesty International, and UN bodies consistently finds that Cameroonian security forces operate with near-total legal immunity for torture, particularly in counter-terrorism and Anglophone conflict operations.

laws.title: Cotton and Textile Industry
laws.subtitle: SODECOTON and Far North Agriculture
laws.fullDescription: SODECOTON (Société de Développement du Coton) manages cotton production in northern Cameroon — providing seeds, inputs, credit, and purchasing to smallholder farmers in the Adamawa and Far North regions. Cotton is a major cash crop for northern farmers. The CICAM (Industrie Cotonnière du Cameroun) textile mill processes local cotton into fabric. Cotton production is affected by Boko Haram insecurity, climate variability (rainfall reduction), and global commodity prices. The integration from farmer to mill represents a rare value chain model in Cameroon agriculture.
laws.penalty: Cotton smuggling across Nigeria border: customs prosecution; SODECOTON input subsidy fraud: criminal prosecution; non-delivery of cotton after advance payment: civil and criminal liability
exceptions: Smallholder farmers within SODECOTON program receive guaranteed minimum price even in low market periods
Emergency price support mechanisms activated during severe commodity price collapses

quiz.q: What does SODECOTON provide to northern Cameroon cotton farmers?
options: Seeds, inputs, credit, and purchase guarantees — managing the full cotton value chain
quiz.explanation: SODECOTON provides an integrated package to northern Cameroon cotton smallholders: seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, credit (repaid at harvest), extension training, and guaranteed purchase at agreed prices. This integrated model — unusual in Cameroonian agriculture — has maintained cotton production in challenging conditions, though Boko Haram insecurity and climate change increasingly threaten it.

laws.title: CEMAC Presidency and Cameroon's Role
laws.subtitle: Regional Leadership and ECCAS
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon, as the largest CEMAC economy, plays a central role in regional organizations. President Biya has held the CEMAC rotational presidency. ECCAS (Economic Community of Central African States) — the broader Central African regional body — includes larger membership. Cameroon has used its position to pursue regional integration despite domestic governance challenges. The CEMAC passport and free movement protocols allow citizens to travel within the zone without visas. Cameroon's Douala port and transit infrastructure make it the practical regional hub regardless of formal leadership positions.
laws.penalty: Violations of CEMAC free movement protocols for regional citizens: administrative sanction — not criminal; ECCAS treaty obligations breach: diplomatic dispute resolution
exceptions: National security grounds allow Cameroon to restrict movement of individuals on security watch lists
Emergency public health restrictions may temporarily override free movement

quiz.q: Why is Cameroon the practical hub of the CEMAC region regardless of formal leadership?
options: It has the most democratic governance
Cameroon's Douala port and transit infrastructure serve all landlocked CEMAC neighbors
It contributes the most to CEMAC budget
It has the strongest military in the region
quiz.explanation: Cameroon is the CEMAC region's practical hub primarily because of the Port of Douala — the main maritime gateway for landlocked Chad, CAR, and northern DRC — and the transit road and rail infrastructure connecting the port to these neighbors. This geographic reality gives Cameroon outsized economic influence in the region regardless of formal leadership rotation.

laws.title: Family Code and Matrimonial Rights
laws.subtitle: Persons and Family Code and Inheritance
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's Code des Personnes et de la Famille governs marriage, divorce, custody, and inheritance. Polygamy is legal under the code — men may have multiple wives under monogamous or polygamous marriage contracts. Inheritance law has gender-discriminatory provisions — widows may be excluded from inheriting family property under customary law despite formal code protections. Marriage requires minimum age (18 for men, 15 for women with parental consent — though 18 is now the standard after child marriage reforms). Divorce processes heavily favor wealthier parties who can afford legal proceedings.
laws.penalty: Forced marriage: criminal prosecution; marriage of underage persons: prosecution of parents and officiants; bigamy under monogamous marriage contract: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Polygamous marriage requires explicit declaration at time of first marriage — converting from monogamous to polygamous after marriage requires court process
Islamic personal law provisions recognized for Muslim communities in northern Cameroon

quiz.q: Is polygamy legal in Cameroon?
options: Legal — men may have multiple wives if declaring polygamous intent at time of first marriage
Only legal in northern Muslim communities
Only practiced traditionally but illegal formally
quiz.explanation: Polygamy is legal in Cameroon under the Code des Personnes et de la Famille — men may marry multiple wives provided they declare their intent for a polygamous marriage (as opposed to a monogamous contract) at the time of their first marriage. Converting from a monogamous to polygamous marriage status after the first marriage requires a court process.

laws.title: Maritime Law and Port Security
laws.subtitle: ISEMAR and Gulf of Guinea Piracy
laws.fullDescription: The Gulf of Guinea — where Cameroon's coast sits — is the world's most dangerous maritime region for piracy. Criminal networks operating primarily from Nigerian waters have attacked vessels off Cameroon's coast, Equatorial Guinea, and Gabon. Cameroon has strengthened its naval capacity. ISEMAR (Regional Center for Maritime Safety and Security in Central Africa) coordinates Gulf of Guinea maritime security. IMO (International Maritime Organization) conventions are ratified by Cameroon. Cameroon participates in the Yaoundé Code of Conduct on maritime security.
laws.penalty: Maritime piracy: life imprisonment; armed robbery at sea: 20–30 years; maritime terrorism: life imprisonment; stowaways on vessels — criminal charges for organizers
exceptions: Sailors exercising self-defense against pirate attacks protected under maritime self-defense doctrine
Coast guard and naval operations have armed intervention authority against pirate vessels

quiz.q: What is the Gulf of Guinea's global maritime security significance?
options: The world's most dangerous maritime region for piracy — where Cameroon's coast is located
quiz.explanation: The Gulf of Guinea is consistently ranked the world's most dangerous maritime region for piracy — with criminal networks (primarily from Nigerian waters) attacking oil tankers, cargo vessels, and fishing boats. Unlike Somali piracy (which declined after naval intervention), Gulf of Guinea piracy has been harder to suppress and involves more violence against crews.

laws.title: Reforestation Programs
laws.subtitle: MINFOF and Carbon Sequestration Projects
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon has ambitious reforestation targets under its NDC (Nationally Determined Contribution) commitments to the Paris Agreement. MINFOF coordinates reforestation programs — including community-based tree planting, natural regeneration support, and agroforestry promotion. Carbon credit projects (REDD+ and VCS/Gold Standard voluntary carbon markets) attract private investment into Cameroon's forests. However, the net deforestation rate remains positive — deforestation exceeds replanting. The challenge is balancing agricultural expansion (food security) with forest conservation (climate commitments).
laws.penalty: Fraudulent carbon credit issuance: criminal fraud prosecution; reforestation fund misappropriation: criminal prosecution; burning of forests without permit: criminal prosecution and restoration order
exceptions: Traditional fire management (burning for agriculture in savanna zones) permitted in designated areas
Emergency salvage logging of storm-damaged trees in plantation areas authorized without normal permit

quiz.q: What are NDCs in relation to Cameroon's forest and climate commitments?
options: National Development Conditions for donor funding
Nationally Determined Contributions — Paris Agreement climate commitments including reforestation targets
quiz.explanation: NDCs (Nationally Determined Contributions) are each country's self-defined commitments under the Paris Agreement. Cameroon's NDC includes reforestation targets, reduced deforestation rates, and emission reduction goals. Meeting these commitments involves balancing forest conservation with agricultural expansion, and accessing international climate finance to fund sustainable alternatives.

laws.title: Journalists and Press Freedom
laws.subtitle: CPJ, RSF Rankings, and Media Law
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's press freedom record is among the worst globally — RSF (Reporters Without Borders) consistently ranks it in the bottom 20 countries. The government uses criminal defamation, cybercrime laws, and anti-terrorism provisions to prosecute journalists. The journalist Mimi Mefo was arrested in 2018 for reporting on military operations in the Anglophone region. Online media faces particularly aggressive prosecution. The Cameroon National Communication Council (CNC) can suspend media outlets. Physical attacks on journalists occur. Despite this environment, Cameroon has active private media including numerous radio stations and online outlets.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation of public officials: 5 years; spreading false news: 3 years; online content causing 'public disorder': Cybercrime Act penalties; terrorism-related journalism charges: 20+ years
exceptions: Parliamentary immunity covers statements made in Parliament and its committees
Diplomatic media entities (VOA, RFI, BBC) have some additional protection through host country agreements

quiz.q: What happened to journalist Mimi Mefo in Cameroon in 2018?
options: She won a press freedom award
She was arrested for reporting on military operations in the Anglophone region
quiz.explanation: Mimi Mefo, a TV journalist with Equinoxe TV, was arrested in November 2018 and charged with 'spreading false information' and 'terrorism' after reporting on military operations in the Anglophone crisis region. Her arrest — and subsequent release following international pressure — became a symbol of Cameroon's aggressive suppression of conflict reporting.

laws.title: Tea Industry Cameroon
laws.subtitle: CDC Tea Estates and Export Markets
laws.fullDescription: The CDC (Cameroon Development Corporation) operates major tea estates in the Southwest Region — particularly in the highland areas near Mount Cameroon where climate and altitude favor tea production. Cameroon tea is exported primarily to the UK and regional markets. Tea production employs thousands of workers — predominantly women. The Anglophone conflict severely disrupted CDC tea operations — with attacks on estates, worker displacement, and harvest disruptions. Tea estates are considered symbols of the colonial economic structure and have been targeted by armed groups. Recovery has been slow.
laws.penalty: Vandalism of agricultural estate infrastructure: criminal prosecution; unauthorized occupation of tea plantation land: criminal prosecution; theft of tea harvest: prosecution
exceptions: Smallholder outgrower tea farmers adjacent to CDC estates have preferential supply agreements
Workers displaced by conflict may claim emergency hardship support under labor law provisions

quiz.q: How has the Anglophone conflict affected Cameroon's tea industry?
options: Boosted tea production as a conflict commodity
Severely disrupted CDC operations — attacks on estates, worker displacement, harvest disruptions
No significant impact — tea is grown in unaffected areas
Caused tea prices to rise benefiting producers
quiz.explanation: The Anglophone conflict severely disrupted Cameroon's CDC tea industry in the Southwest Region — with armed groups attacking tea estates (seen as colonial economic symbols), displacing workers, preventing harvests, and damaging infrastructure. Production has fallen sharply from pre-conflict levels, causing significant economic harm to the thousands of workers and communities depending on tea employment.

laws.title: State of Emergency Powers
laws.subtitle: Emergency Laws and Crisis Governance
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's constitution allows the President to declare a State of Emergency — conferring extraordinary powers to restrict movement, assembly, and rights. States of emergency have been declared in the Far North (Boko Haram) and portions of the Anglophone regions. During COVID-19, emergency health measures were implemented. Emergency powers have been used to justify military tribunal jurisdiction over civilians, extended detention, and restrictions on humanitarian access. International law (including ICCPR) permits emergency derogations — but only to the extent strictly required by the situation.
laws.penalty: Violation of emergency curfew: immediate arrest and detention; organizing prohibited gatherings during emergency: criminal prosecution; impeding emergency forces: 5–10 years
exceptions: Non-derogable rights — prohibition on torture, right to life — cannot be suspended even during emergency
Humanitarian operations continue under emergency with special coordination protocols

quiz.q: What rights cannot be suspended even during a declared State of Emergency in Cameroon?
options: All rights can be suspended during emergency
Non-derogable rights including prohibition on torture and right to life
Only property rights are protected during emergency
Only the president's powers are constrained
quiz.explanation: International human rights law (and Cameroon's constitutional framework) identifies non-derogable rights that cannot be suspended even during states of emergency — including the absolute prohibition on torture, the right to life, and freedom from arbitrary execution. These protections remain binding even when Cameroon activates emergency powers in the Far North or Anglophone regions.

laws.title: Tourism Potential and Ecotourism
laws.subtitle: MINTOUR and Wildlife Tourism Development
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon is sometimes called 'Africa in miniature' — containing rainforest, savanna, mountains, desert-edge, and Atlantic coast ecosystems within its borders. Tourism potential is enormous but largely unrealized. The MINTOUR (Ministry of Tourism) coordinates development. Wildlife tourism in Waza, Benoué, and other parks could generate significant revenue. Beach tourism around Limbe and Kribi has growing appeal. The Anglophone crisis severely damaged tourism to the Northwest and Southwest. Political instability, security concerns, and limited infrastructure have constrained foreign tourist arrivals. Ecotourism projects involve local community benefit-sharing.
laws.penalty: Operating unregistered tourism business: fines and closure; wildlife tourism guides without license: fines; tourist fraud: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Community-based tourism initiatives under MINTOUR partnership agreements have simplified licensing
Volunteer tourism programs under registered NGOs exempt from commercial tourism regulations

quiz.q: Why is Cameroon sometimes called 'Africa in miniature'?
options: It is geographically the center of Africa
It contains rainforest, savanna, mountains, desert-edge, and Atlantic coast — representing Africa's full diversity
It has populations from all African ethnic groups
It is exactly 1/54th of Africa's land area
quiz.explanation: Cameroon is called 'Africa in miniature' because its compact territory contains the full spectrum of African ecological zones: Congo Basin rainforest (south), Guinea savanna (west highlands), Sudan-Sahel savanna and semi-desert (north), Mount Cameroon's alpine zones, and Atlantic beaches (coast) — making it one of the most ecologically diverse countries on the continent.

laws.title: Industrial Pollution and Remediation
laws.subtitle: MINEPDED Standards and Corporate Liability
laws.fullDescription: Industrial pollution in Cameroon — particularly around Douala's industrial zones (Bassa, Bonabéri) — affects communities, water sources, and air quality. Effluent discharge from manufacturing into the Wouri estuary has damaged fisheries and water quality. MINEPDED (Ministry of Environment) sets pollution standards and conducts inspections. Environmental impact assessments (EIAs) are required for major industrial projects. Industrial accidents — chemical spills, factory fires — create acute pollution events. Enforcement is uneven — small operators may face more scrutiny than politically connected large companies.
laws.penalty: Illegal industrial effluent discharge: fines up to CFA 100M and remediation orders; atmospheric emissions violations: 3× violation fines and factory shutdown; environmental crime by corporate directors: personal criminal liability
exceptions: Industrial companies under MINEPDED rehabilitation plan have extended compliance timelines
Legacy pollution predating environmental regulations subject to negotiated remediation rather than criminal prosecution

quiz.q: Where is Cameroon's main industrial concentration causing environmental concerns?
options: Douala's industrial zones (Bassa, Bonabéri) — affecting the Wouri estuary
In the Far North oil fields
quiz.explanation: Douala's industrial zones — Bassa and Bonabéri — concentrate manufacturing activities including chemicals, food processing, and light industry. Effluent from these zones discharges into the Wouri estuary, damaging fisheries that support thousands of livelihoods and affecting drinking water quality for coastal communities. Industrial environmental enforcement in these zones is challenged by political and economic pressures.

laws.title: Online Political Speech and Censorship
laws.subtitle: CNC, ANTIC, and Digital Rights
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon uses multiple tools to control online political speech: criminal defamation laws, the 2010 Cybersecurity Law, the 2015 Penal Code provisions on false news, and internet shutdowns. ANTIC (National Agency for IT) monitors online content. Bloggers and social media users have been prosecuted for criticizing government officials. Facebook and WhatsApp groups have been monitored for political organizing. The 2017-2018 internet shutdown in Anglophone regions was one of Africa's longest. International digital rights organizations have documented systematic suppression of online dissent.
laws.penalty: Online defamation of public official: 5 years (Cybersecurity Act); false information spreading: 3 years; online incitement to insurrection: 10–20 years; publishing 'subversive' content: 5–15 years
exceptions: Academic discussion of policy without direct defamatory accusations — gray area in practice
Satirical content — theoretically protected but prosecuted in practice in Cameroon

quiz.q: What was historically significant about the 2017-2018 internet shutdown in Cameroon's Anglophone regions?
options: It was the first internet shutdown anywhere in the world
At approximately 93 days it was one of Africa's longest internet shutdowns at that time
It was legally challenged and overturned by courts
quiz.explanation: The 2017-2018 internet shutdown in Cameroon's Northwest and Southwest Anglophone regions lasted approximately 93 days — making it one of the longest in African history at that time. The shutdown was imposed in response to Anglophone protests and caused massive economic damage while cutting communities from information, healthcare telemedicine, and financial services.

laws.title: Artisanal Gold Mining (ASGM)
laws.subtitle: CAPAM and Mercury Pollution
laws.fullDescription: Artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) in Cameroon — primarily in the Adamawa, East, and South regions — employs hundreds of thousands informally. CAPAM (Centre d'Assistance aux Artisans Miniers) supports formalization. Mercury use in ASGM for gold amalgamation creates serious environmental and health hazards — mercury pollution contaminates rivers and fish consumed by local communities. Cameroon has ratified the Minamata Convention on Mercury — committing to reducing mercury use in ASGM. Child labor in ASGM is documented. Formalization efforts face challenges from deep informal sector entrenchment.
laws.penalty: Mercury use beyond Minamata Convention protocols: fines and equipment seizure; child labor in mining: 5–15 years; operating ASGM without CAPAM registration: fines and closure
exceptions: Mercury-free gold processing methods encouraged under CAPAM technical assistance — operators transitioning to mercury-free methods receive reduced penalties
Traditional river gold panning below commercial scale has informal toleration

quiz.q: What environmental treaty has Cameroon ratified to address mercury in gold mining?
options: Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants
quiz.explanation: Cameroon has ratified the Minamata Convention on Mercury — the international treaty specifically targeting mercury pollution, named after the Japanese city devastated by mercury poisoning. For Cameroon, the key obligation is reducing mercury use in artisanal gold mining (ASGM), where mercury amalgamation remains common despite serious health and environmental hazards.

laws.title: Technical and Vocational Education
laws.subtitle: MINEFOP and Skills Development
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) system — managed by MINEFOP (Ministry of Employment and Vocational Training) — aims to provide skills for the labor market. Technical schools, Centers for Technical and Vocational Education (CETACs), and apprenticeship programs train youth in trades, agriculture, and technical skills. Youth unemployment is very high — particularly for university graduates whose qualifications don't match available jobs. The mismatch between university output and labor market needs is a persistent challenge. Dual training programs involving private sector employers are being expanded.
laws.penalty: Operating unaccredited vocational training institution: fines and closure; falsifying vocational certificates: criminal prosecution; labor law violations by apprenticeship employers: fines
exceptions: Informal apprenticeship under traditional master-artisan relationships recognized under MINEFOP informal economy programs
Community skills training by NGOs under MINEFOP partnership agreements has simplified authorization

quiz.q: What challenge exists between Cameroon's university output and labor market?
options: Too few university graduates for available professional jobs
Significant mismatch — university graduates' qualifications don't match available jobs, creating high graduate unemployment
Universities produce graduates too quickly for employers to absorb
Language barriers prevent graduates from working across the country
quiz.explanation: Cameroon faces a significant skills mismatch — large numbers of university graduates are unemployed because their qualifications don't match available labor market needs, while employers struggle to find workers with practical, vocational skills. This mismatch has led to expansion of TVET (Technical and Vocational Education and Training) as an alternative to university education.

laws.title: National Anti-Corruption Legislation
laws.subtitle: Law 3/2006 and Ethics Commission
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon's main anti-corruption legislation — Law 3/2006 on asset declaration and law on the financing of political parties — requires senior public officials to declare assets. The National Commission for the Prevention of Corruption (CONAC) monitors compliance. Asset declaration is often not publicly accessible, limiting accountability. Political party financing is opaque — parties largely funded by individual backers rather than transparent mechanisms. Civil society anti-corruption organizations face restrictions on their work. International anti-corruption frameworks (UNCAC) are ratified but compliance is partial.
laws.penalty: Failure to declare assets when required: administrative sanction and fine; false asset declaration: criminal prosecution; illegal party financing: fines and party deregistration threat
exceptions: Security personnel may redact sensitive operational assets from public declarations
Classified state assets excluded from transparency requirements

quiz.q: What does Law 3/2006 require of senior Cameroonian public officials?
options: Asset declaration — disclosing their wealth and financial interests
quiz.explanation: Law 3/2006 requires senior Cameroonian public officials — including ministers, senior civil servants, and parliamentarians — to declare their assets. The system is intended to detect illicit enrichment. However, enforcement is limited — declarations are not always publicly accessible, compliance is uneven, and CONAC has limited independence to act against politically protected officials.

laws.title: Banana Industry Regulations
laws.subtitle: PHP and CDC Banana Exports to Europe
laws.fullDescription: Cameroon is a significant banana exporter to Europe — producing Cavendish bananas primarily through PHP (Plantations du Haut Penja) and CDC estates. PHP is one of Cameroon's largest private agricultural employers. European markets require strict phytosanitary certification and compliance with EU food safety standards. The ACP-EU Banana Trade Agreement provides preferential market access.
